title: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
description_short: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
description_medium: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 revising federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including recommending separate administration of MMR components once available and spacing immunizations across visits. In remarks at the signing, Trump said the initiative involved autism and reiterated claims linking childhood vaccination practices to autism. Major medical and scientific reviews, including a 2025-2026 WHO evidence review, found no causal relationship between vaccines and autism.
description_long: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420, which revised federal recommendations for childhood vaccines and directed further review. The supplied correction says the order recommended giving MMR components separately once available and spacing immunizations across visits. At the signing, Trump said the initiative involved autism and repeated claims linking childhood vaccination practices to autism. The order’s policy changes and the president’s remarks are distinct: the executive order did not establish a scientific causal link between vaccines and autism. A World Health Organization evidence review covering research through 2025 found that the most rigorous evidence did not support such a causal association. The event therefore combined a federal change to vaccine recommendations with rhetoric about autism that conflicts with the review’s conclusion. The date in the packet’s corrected title and description is August 10, 2026, although the record’s date_start remains August 1, 2025.

title: Trump Seeks Supreme Court Approval for Controversial White House Renovation
description_short: Trump Seeks Supreme Court Approval for Controversial White House Renovation
description_medium: On August 14, 2026, Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court to let work resume on a $400 million White House ballroom project at the demolished East Wing site. The request followed a D.C. Circuit decision upholding a stop-work order. The administration cited national security, while the National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that the case concerned compliance with the rule of law.
description_long: The dispute concerns a $400 million ballroom project planned for the White House East Wing site. After the East Wing was demolished, the National Trust for Historic Preservation sued, and a federal district judge issued a preliminary injunction pausing construction while the case proceeded. On August 7, 2026, the D.C. Circuit upheld the stop-work order. A week later, Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court to set aside that order so construction could continue. The administration’s filing described the project as a national-security necessity and argued that a secure ballroom would serve presidential safety. The National Trust opposed the request and said the administration should not evade judicial review. The petition asked the Supreme Court for permission to resume work; the linked report does not state that the Court granted it. The episode put a construction project and the scope of executive discretion before the courts, with the lower-court order set to take effect on August 21 unless the justices intervened.

title: Trump's Grab for Power and Secrecy
description_short: Trump's Grab for Power and Secrecy
description_medium: A Trump administration memo asserted that executive privilege protects presidential communications with private advisers who are not government employees. In an August 2026 opinion piece, law professor Noah Feldman argued that the claim departed from the traditional scope of the privilege, which covers communications within government. The issue could affect congressional investigations, but the article described a legal position, not a court ruling.
description_long: The Trump administration’s Office of Legal Counsel issued a memo asserting that executive privilege could protect the president’s communications with private advisers outside government. In an August 17, 2026, opinion article, Harvard law professor Noah Feldman argued that the privilege had traditionally applied to communications between the president and public officials, not private citizens. He said the claim could shield conversations with outside advisers from congressional subpoenas, including inquiries into potential conflicts or private dealings. The memo relied in part on an earlier Office of Legal Counsel opinion about communications with members of Congress involved in confirming U.S. attorneys, a context Feldman said did not justify extending the privilege to private advisers generally. The dispute concerns the boundary between confidential presidential advice and Congress’s investigative authority. The article is legal commentary criticizing the memo; it does not report a court decision resolving the question. Any future privilege claim would still have to be asserted in a specific congressional dispute and tested through the legal process.

title: Trump Regulators Let Trump Firm Start a Bank
description_short: Trump Regulators Let Trump Firm Start a Bank
description_medium: CNN reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency had given World Liberty Financial preliminary conditional approval to become a trust bank. Final approval depended on additional conditions, and the proposed bank could not take deposits or make loans. Lawmakers and watchdogs raised conflict-of-interest concerns because the crypto firm was founded by the Trump family.
description_long: World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company launched by Donald Trump and his sons, announced that it had received preliminary conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to become a trust bank. The approval was not final: the company still had to meet conditions. The proposed bank would not be able to take deposits or make loans, but it could safeguard and issue World Liberty’s USD1 dollar-backed stablecoin. CNN reported that the charter could reduce the company’s reliance on outside intermediaries. A Trump family entity, DT Marks SC LLC, agreed to be a passive investor and not participate in the bank’s operations; Eric Trump signed that agreement. Ethics watchdogs and lawmakers nevertheless warned that a federal regulator’s approval of a bank tied to the president’s family created a conflict of interest. The episode was a conditional regulatory step, not authorization for a fully operating deposit-taking bank. The article reported that final approval remained contingent on further conditions.
organization_tags: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
